- Last month we noted the lack of direction in copper prices, with as many reasons to be optimistic being negated by just as many urging for caution.  This month the bears have won out, with LME cash averaging US$8890/t ($4.03/lb) thus far in May compared with April’s US$9483/t ($4.30/lb).  In our view, this has only been partly driven by the traditional supply-demand fundamentals, given the paucity of noteworthy information or any significant change to circumstances. 

- Minor changes to our refined metal forecasts since our last report for 2011 (+57kt) and 2012 (-76kt) when placed against our demand revisions (+92kt and +280kt for 2011 and 2012, respectively) have resulted in slightly tighter markets for these two years.  However, the price dip seen this month has required a small reduction in our forecast price for this year, from US$9861/t ($4.47/lb) to US$9586/t ($4.35/lb).  We should emphasise, however, that we still envisage a more positive price environment for the second half of this year. 

- One exceedingly bearish element this year has been the high level of Chinese bonded warehouse stocks (600-700kt) that has cast a great shadow over the market thus far in 2011.  Our understanding is that during April and May the overall bonded inventory has been reduced by approximately 50%.  This would explain China’s ongoing lacklustre trade in refined metal.  Therefore, the real picture in April/May has been considerably more upbeat when one adds on to Chinese consumption the additional 150kt/m from bonded metal stocks and a further 45kt/m from Shanghai warehouse inventories in each month.  This also explains why we show a significant Q2 metal deficit in our balances. 

- According to trade rumour, BHP Billiton, acting on behalf of Escondida, has recently concluded TC/RC deals with smelting companies in India, China and Japan at $90/t & 9c/lb.  The Chilean miner broke with tradition during the last Mating Season when it gave buyers the option to price their annual concentrate purchases on the basis of a standard annual TC/RC benchmark or to negotiate terms biannually with reference to prevailing spot market terms.

## Market Developments 

**Copper prices trend down over May** Last month we noted the lack of direction in copper prices, with as many reasons to be optimistic being negated by just as many urging for caution.  This month the bears have won out, with LME cash averaging US$8890/t ($4.03/lb) thus far in May compared with April’s US$9483/t ($4.30/lb).  In our view, this has only been partly driven by the traditional supply-demand fundamentals, given the paucity of noteworthy information or any significant change to circumstances.  What we have noticed more so this month is active involvement of investment banks promoting their views on metal demand and the impact they have had on prices.  Initially, this was quite bearish, and in late April there was a widespread opinion pushing for a commodities sell-off – including copper.  More recently, this opinion has been reversed, and the impacts on both occasions of these views have become self-fulfilling prophecies. Consequently, we saw copper open this month at US$9243/t ($4.19/lb) – continuing the slide which began on April 21<sup>st</sup> – to find a floor of US$8536/t ($3.87/lb – cash) on May 12<sup>th</sup> , the lowest prices since late-November/early December last year.  The subsequent correction came only with a shift in the dollar’s direction and with some “encouraging” SHFE:LME arbitrage circumstances. 

**Long liquidation drives May’s price decline** But, as we noted above, May’s metal price behaviour has largely been technically driven by the views and actions of financial institutions.  Open interest data for copper in May suggests that this month’s correction in prices was the result of significant long liquidation.  A similar pattern took place in other base metals, and was reflective of a shift away from risk assets across the financial markets.  The fact that the drop for copper and other base metals was driven by long liquidation is important, as it represents the cashing in of gains in price made since mid- 2010.  Such long liquidation is limited by the number of positions available to be closed out, and together with the fact that new shorts do not yet seem to have become prevalent, it indicates that what we have seen in the past month is more likely to have been more of a correction than the beginning of a downward spiral in metal prices. 

**“Encouraging” Chinese arbitrage window** From that May 12<sup>th</sup> price low, copper pushed up consistently for the next seven trading days, and even returned to the US$9000/t level ($4.08/lb) on the 19<sup>th</sup> .  What prompted that mini-surge during this period was the reopening of the arbitrage window between the LME and China’s SHFE, which has been increasingly apparent over the last two months.  As this persisted, the market reacted favourably to the implications that this scenario brings, namely a reversal of Chinese exports of refined metal (into LME warehouses), and the potential for renewed Chinese metal buying.  This came at

a time when other circumstances suggested that at least some of this renewed buying in China would actually be for metal consumption purposes rather than merely for financial motives (i.e. holding metal stock as collateral against borrowing funds for non metal-related needs). **Lower Chinese metal imports in April…** One exceedingly bearish element this year has been the high level of Chinese bonded warehouse stocks, which has cast a great shadow over the market thus far in 2011. In the absence of hard figures, the general view is that these stocks rose over the course of Q1 to a peak level of 600-700kt. However, our understanding is that during April and May the overall bonded inventory has been reduced by approximately 50%. This would explain China’s ongoing lacklustre trade in refined metal: April’s imports were down by over 48% year on year, a figure that was (understandably) viewed with considerable pessimism by the market. However, the real picture in April/May has been considerably more upbeat when one adds on to Chinese consumption the additional 150kt/m from bonded metal stocks and a further 45kt/m from Shanghai warehouse inventories each month. **Stocks elsewhere continue to rise** As we noted above, though, China has been exporting copper largely into LME warehouses in Asia, and we will need more time to see whether the recent observations of a reversal to this trend will become a longer-standing feature in the market (much will depend on the SHFE:LME price arbitrage). Although LME stocks increased again this month, it is noticeable that the _rate_ of increase has slowed. Ending April at 463.7kt, only a net additional 6kt had entered LME warehouses by May 26th _vs._ a net inflow average of 21.8kt/month since last December. Most of this increase seen in May came at warehouses in Singapore (40.8kt _vs._ 34.7kt at end-April) and Malaysia (6.1kt at Port Klang _vs._ 2.0kt a month ago); meanwhile, stocks in South Korea were reasonably stable compared with recent months, down by only 300t across the three sites. Elsewhere, Comex warehouse inventories have edged down for the second consecutive month and are now 73.5kt (as of May 26th ). Metals Market Service Monthly Update - May 2011 Page 3 of 23 Copper Monthly Update **General economic data less than helpful in sustaining metals prices** The fact that stocks have been slow to move out of their warehouses outside China also proved an impediment to prices remaining above the US$9000/t mark ($4.08/lb) on a consistent basis since that May 19th date, even if the final days in the month are once again revisiting those levels. Equally, concern over European country debt levels, and renewed discussion over the ability of the USA to build upon its slim Q1 growth rate of just 0.4% ( _vs._ the 3.1% hike seen in Q4 2010) are also hanging over a nervous market. Furthermore, even though most countries’ PMI’s have remained above the 50 growth level, they have fallen of late (e.g. China’s 51.1 preliminary figure for April), raising concerns for demand growth in the near term. **Chinese buying will offset the summer recess in the West** As we enter the traditional summer slowdown in the northern hemisphere, it is unlikely that we will read of a consistent upswing in metal demand, and in theory we should anticipate lower prices ahead. However, this time around it might not be so straightforward. As noted, pent up Chinese demand and declining domestic inventories indicate to us that their metal import requirements should rise in the coming months, and if the indicators aired above persist into June, then this alone wi

ll be sufficient to overturn edginess and doubt in western countries during the summer industrial recess. The one grey area on this is the aspect of supposed power restrictions in China this summer. But so far this is pure conjecture, as no consuming metal sector has yet stated that it will have an impact on business levels. **All eyes on Asarco as we head into June** Equally, even in the USA there are some specific circumstances which could provide support to copper prices that would be unexpected. We refer here to the Asarco group, which produces 200kt/a of mined copper whose labour contracts expire on June 30th at all of its operations in the southwest, from mines through to its Amarillo rod mill. Already, other rod mills from the southern states through to Nexans in eastern Canada are eagerly awaiting any opportunity to fill the gap left by a struck Amarillo plant. **Slight revisions to the fundamentals leave us with tighter markets through to 2013** Minor changes to our refined metal forecasts since our last report for 2011 (+57kt) and 2012 (-76kt) when placed against our demand revisions (+92kt and +280kt for 2011 and 2012, respectively) have resulted in slightly tighter markets for these two years. However, the price dip seen this month has required a small reduction in our forecast price for this year, from US$9861/t ($4.47/lb) to US$9586/t ($4.35/lb). We should emphasise, however, that we still envisage a more positive price environment for the second half of this year. China’s inventory adjustment that commenced in September last year, has resulted in a substantial decline in pipeline stocks along its consumption chain. Modest end-use demand growth during H2 is all that will be needed to drive up refined consumption due to the magnifying effect of restocking between the end use and first use markets. The lower metal stock days of consumption (43 _vs._ 56) now anticipated for 2012 has prompted us to increase our forecast price for next year, though, from a prior US$9150/t ($4.15/lb) to US$9588/t ($4.35/lb). Equally, the near 1Mt surplus previously expected in 2013 now stands at <550kt, and the consequent reduction in stock days of consumption is likely to leave prices somewhat closer to the four-dollar average than our prior $3.58/lb. #### **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

## Consumption 

The Chinese market remains in focus this month as declining stocks and firm premia point to improving demand conditions, while there was even some restocking at downstream producers amid the dip in cathode price levels.  Semis output is on the up but clouds are gathering in the shape of power shortages in the summer, which could crimp production levels and in doing so temper Chinese refined demand.  However, we remain confident on the near term outlook for China and, indeed, elsewhere.  Meanwhile, European demand remains firm, although evidence of substitution continues to emerge, while activity in North America continues to be relatively calm. 

### **Europe and CIS** 

**Signs emerge of Euro area economic slowdown** Signs are emerging that the recent strength in euro area economic growth (in the core anyway) has lost momentum.  Euro zone industrial output contracted in March from the prior month, owing largely to a drop in France.  The latest PMI data suggests that growth will continue, albeit at a lower pace, with the preliminary euro zone PMI falling from 57.8 in April to a seven month low of 55.4, led by dips in both the manufacturing and services sub-indices.  Even Germany does not appear to be immune to the slowing, with the German index dropping from 59.2 to 56.4 in the May reading. 

**Semis output maintains solid pace** Overall output of copper semis has maintained a solid pace, with wire rod in particular driving healthy demand for refined material, although in other segments the high cost of cathode is triggering substitution and leading to a softening in output.  Wire rod producers continue to report healthy order books and longer than usual lead times amid continued firm demand across the sectors.  However, tube makers, along with sheet and strip producers note that bookings are being tempered by the still relatively lofty price of copper which is driving end users to less expensive materials. 

**European premia hold firm** Cathode premia have remained in line with last month at around the $75/t mark for grade A material.  Although there have been the odd fluctuations here and there, premia have held firm at similar levels for the past few months now, after spiking at the start of the year as cathode availability tightened as Russian exports turned lower following the re-imposition of tax on overseas shipments.

**Automotive market slows further** In a warning shot across the bow of rod orders, however, the European car market continues to bump along, with many markets still suffering from the hangover of scrapping incentive schemes. While automotive production in key market Germany still maintained year-on-year growth in April, up by 1.6%, UK production slumped by 13% amid parts supply difficulties at Japanese marque factories. As we have said before though, production growth in Germany is the key market for copper demand owing to its abundance of metals-intensive luxury brands. **Aurubis buys Luvata** Aurubis is to buy the rolled copper division of Luvata in a deal set to cost the firm around €200250m. Both parties seem to be happy with the transaction as it allows Aurubis to break into the downstream US market and also strengthen its position in semis in Europe, while for Luvata the deal will allow them to focus on higher value products. **Aurubis Q1 rod production outpaces shapes** Meanwhile, Aurubis has released its latest quarterly production data, which revealed strong growth in wire rod output but a sharp slide in shapes. Indeed, wire rod production rose by 11.3% year on year to 217kt and marking the second consecutive quarter-on-quarter increase. However, output of shapes fell on a year-on-year and quarter-on-quarter basis, down by 17.9% to 46kt. This is in line with our discussions with market participants who report strong demand for wire rod but that high copper prices are starting to temper growth in areas such us tubes and sheet and strip. Output overall was higher by 4.8% year on year to 263kt and fits comfortably with our full year Western European refined demand forecast. This seems consistent with most recent macro data. US industrial activity contracted marginally in April, owing entirely to a seasonally adjusted 12.5% drop in automotive output (parts shortages). **Auto sector output falls heavily in April…** The automotive sector has been suffering more than most would have credited only a couple of months ago: total vehicle production in the US dropped by 12% month on month in April, and some of this is due to parts shortages following on from the Japanese natural disaster. Year on year growth fell from 20% in March to 2.3%, taking growth for the first four months to 12.3%. Anecdotal evidence suggests that US output is unlikely to get back to “normal” levels before the end of Q2. As of yet, we have retained our 2011 forecasts for production growth of 7.4% in the US. **..even if auto sales remain strong** In contrast to production, vehicle sales in April continued to expand at a solid rate, with total sales of 1.176m units up by 17.9% y-o-y. However, such growth does not appear likely to persist. Incentive schemes have decreased massively since the start of the year to their lowest rate in over 5 years, and high oil prices are denting consumer spending plans. Preliminary data suggest that sales in May could fall by over 10% from April. Having said that, the US Energy Department thinks that gasoline prices may have peaked already, and both vehicle production and sales should improve in H2. **Manufacturing stalls in April, likely to dip in the short-term** US manufacturing should resume growth in the coming months, but faces some headwinds. Auto output will be constrained in the short term by ongoing parts issues, and domestic investment looks to be subdued. This is reflected in the US PMI, the new orders component of which fell from 68 back in Feb to 61.7 in April, suggesting slowe

r growth over the short term. 

**Non-residential construction picks up…** In the buildings and construction markets, the improvement in March’s housing starts data proved to be short lived.  Starts fell by 10.6% m-o-m and 23% y-o-y in April to an annualised rate of 523,000 units (~1/4 of the peak from the 2005 boom).  The massive overhang of foreclosed properties still to come onto the already oversupplied market will continue to weigh on new residential construction, keeping volumes at these very low levels through into next year.  The Architects Billing Index improved very modestly in March for the 3<sup>rd</sup> straight month, continuing to suggest that slight improvements in non-residential construction volumes should be expected from the end of the year. 

Clearly the residential construction markets remain grounded, but there has been some uplift in the building segment from the commercial side.  Stronger retail sales and longer wait times at restaurants are reflective of a public feeling generally more secure about their own personal economy even if unemployment rates remain stubbornly high, and this is converting into renewed confidence by the restaurant trade to press ahead with expansion plans that were not so long ago placed on hold.  Equally, there has been a good amount of “replacement” business following the severe (and ongoing) storm damage that has been plaguing the mid-west and some southern states over the past six weeks or so. This is providing what strength there is to the general building wire and tube markets, and will have to continue doing so until residential construction comes back into play. 

**..and Encore Wire benefits from the improved situation** McKinney, TX-based Encore Wire, which serves both the commercial and residential wire markets, had a much improved first quarter, recording a 28.9% increase year on year in copper wire volumes shipped.  Even so, its 2010 annual report also notes that last year’s unit sales volume, in terms of tonnes of copper wire sold, were 3.8% down on those of 2009, and that year’s shipments were 15.6% down on 2008’s (which were also 12% down on 2007’s), so there is clearly some way to go yet before the construction sector returns to

pre-crisis levels.  That said, Encore reported net sales of $303.4M for Q1 2011 vs. $175.2M a year ago, and realized a much improved spread between the cost of copper purchased for its rod mill and the price of wire sold. 

**But current markets reflect quiet Q2** In the markets, the fact that cathode spot premia rates lifted from year-end 5.0c/lb to 6.0-6.5c/lb through the first quarter were more reflective of higher freight charges due to competition from other products rather than the rude health of copper markets per se.  As mid-west premia now float down towards the 4.55.0c/lb range, the sheer mediocrity of copper business levels is once again shining through

.  With the onset of the traditional summer slowdown just around the corner, there was little optimism at two recent copper-related events in North America (Interwire/Continuous Casting Forum in Atlanta, GA and the American Copper Council’s May meeting in Montreal) that business activity would pick up this side of H1, but a general consensus that late Q3 would exhibit some renewed, if limited, interest. 

**More rod plants on the way?** Two and a half years on from the widespread economic collapse of Q4 2008, and it is surprising to us that we have only seen two wire rod mill closures (Freeport’s Chicago plant and SuperiorEssex’s Vincennes, IN) in what is generally accepted as a market with excess capacity.  Indeed, this year we have even reported on a new rod mill investment from SDI:LaFarga Lacambra and a new tube mill by China’s Hunan Golden Dragon, and this would seem to run counter to the sentiment as expressed by some longer-standing members of the US manufacturing industry.  However, on closer scrutiny, these new plants reflect upstream circumstances that are quite specific to the investors or shareholders themselves.  And, judging by several comments we picked up from downstream wire manufacturers, at least, these new semis players just might find a willing home for their goods, too. 

Some wire rod buyers are unhappy about what they see as an “unfavourable” concentration of power by rod suppliers. For wire drawers of a “medium” size consuming c.1kt/month of rod, there is a growing impetus to integrate backwards by investing in their own cathode melt shop and rod caster, thereby having a wider choice available to them of cathode suppliers instead.  At such a size, the prospect of having large-scale/high-throughput facilities such as those made by Southwire Continuous Rod would be inappropriate, and so this would let in technologies put forward by other suppliers, such as UpCast or Rautomead, which specialize in plants ranging between 3-12kt/a capacity.  The wiredrawers would also like to have the flexibility of using scrap as well as cathode, and so this could attract La Farga Lacambra and Continuus Properzi technology as well.  Either way, going forward we would not be surprised to see rod or tube capacity additions despite the existing over-capacity situation in the North American market. 

### **China** 

**Chinese industrial activity eases off** Growth in Chinese industrial output slowed from 14.8% in March to 13.4% in April, with the drop largely accounted for by oil related industries (transport, chemicals, refining, and plastics).  Given that our IP forecast for the year is 13.1%, the slowdown brings China out of overheating territory, and is not a cause for concern as of yet. 

Leading indicators suggest the slowdown will continue in the next couple of months.  The preliminary China PMI for May fell to a 10-month low of 51.1 from 51.8 in April, still above the expansionary threshold but pointing to slower expansion. The data spook

ed markets, which were already concerned about elevated inflation.  Not that this makes sense, as cooling down ought to help to control inflation. 

**Developments point to demand strength** There have been a number of developments this month that point to firmer refined copper demand in the months to come.  Significantly, stocks continue to decline in SHFE warehouses, with inventories down by just under 40kt from the end of April to the third week of May, while as mentioned we also understand that bonded warehouse stocks have also been in decline and now stand at around 300-400kt, down from 600-700kt only a couple of months ago. 

**Firm premia underscore rising demand** In tandem, local premia have remained firm, in line with tighter availability of material and now stand at the $120/t level.  Although the initial surge in premia to upwards of $100/t that we have discussed previously was down to Japanese producers and traders buying material in a bid to meet their commitments following disruptions in the wake of their earthquake, it is the recent upturn in Chinese semis output has led firmer demand for cathode.  In addition, the recent price “correction” that we discuss elsewhere in this report saw Chinese semis producers take the opportunity for further restocking, and this also contributed to declining stocks and solid premia. 

**Apparent consumption figures yet to reflect improvements** This should all point to improving apparent consumption, although this isn’t showing through in the data yet.  By our calculations using CNIA data, apparent consumption fell by 9.4% year on year in April, hit by the squeeze from net trade despite refined output reportedly up by 13% year on year in April, with the decline in unreported bonded warehouse stocks not showing up in apparent demand.  Imports fell sharply this month, down by 48.3% year on year to 160.2kt, while exports surged by a staggering 800% to 44.6kt.  Exports of refined material, while relatively low in absolute terms have soared compared to the prior year as traders shipped material out of bonded warehouses and into nearby LME warehouses in South Korea and Singapore because of the negative arbitrage between the LME and SHFE.  However, the arbitrage window has been open lately and this should lead to improving imports and declining exports and as such, net trade’s drag on apparent consumption will dissipate in

Still, calculations from CNIA data reveal that in the first four months of the year apparent consumption was down nearly 7%.  This compares with reported semis production down by 1.2% over the same period.  The difference between the two figures must therefore be either unreported stock changes or increased consumption of scrap by semis producers. We b

elieve both are true and have discussed over several months the stock build in copper scrap towards the end of last year in anticipation of VAT rebate changes.  If we add on around 150 kt of consumption from bonded warehouse stocks to the year to date apparent consumption calculation then we get a decline of only 0.6% in the first four months of the year, which tallies much more closely with the reported semis production data.  However, it is important to note that we base these calculations on the numbers reported at the time and do not use the CNIA’s growth rates which are much more healthy but not entirely believable. 

**Solid near term outlook but storm clouds gathering for power** The factors above all point to improving refined demand in the months to come, while our discussions with market participants also confirm the upturn in activity at semis producers and end users.  However, the major negative, putting microeconomic developments to one side, is the potential for power shortages in the summer.  Semis producers, particularly those in Zhejiang province, face a power squeeze during the summer which could hit output.  Clearly, this would have negative implications for refined demand. 

**Semis output powered by wire rod** Wire rod production increased by around 10-15% in May from a month earlier as strong air conditioner production in this period underpinned demand for magnet wire.  In addition, the falling trend of investment in the power grid was reversed in April.  Taking the first four months together, investment in the power grid increased by 4% on the same period a year ago after a solid rise in April’s investment number.  The increased investment supported demand for power cable, although demand for building wire remains flat in line with the overhang of unsold properties in the market. 

**Tube makers at full tilt amid red hot AC production…** Most ACR tube producers ran at full capacity in May in line with strong air conditioner production.  ACR tube production in the first half of this year is estimated to be up in the region of 25-30%, although the full year outlook is more dependent on a hot summer than on cooling measures from central bankers.  Meanwhile, sheet and strip order levels increased by around 10% from April, mainly driven by the increased demand from power cable, screening strip and transformer strip, although demand of connector and lead frame are flat compared to April. 

**…although auto market into the slow lane** The expiration of purchasing incentives, restrictions on registrations in cities such as Beijing and high oil prices have all hit the Chinese auto market so far in 2011.  Both vehicle sales and registrations fell in April in year on year terms for the first time since January 2009, by 0.2% and 1.8% respectively.  Over the first four months, total production is up by just 4.9%.  In line with this, auto related products such as electronic connectors, tyre valves, and wire harness also ebbed lower. The

extent of the slowdown seems to be greater than Chinese officials were expecting, and while growth should resume in the second half, our forecast of a 9% expansion for automobile production in 2011 still seems realistic. **Substitution threatens brass mill output** There was no discernable uplift in order activity at brass rod mills in May and in fact bookings fell from the prior month. Declining exports of sanitary and bathroom hard wares, low demand from the building industry and substitution are major reasons impacting brass rod demand. **Raised outlook for 2012 but we stand firm on 6% this year** While the factors discussed above are particularly positive for near term cathode purchasing, there is a cautious undertone to underlying demand from key sectors such as construction and also transportation. Overall, we are comfortable that these developments are in line with our full year refined demand forecast of 6%, which we have maintained. We have upgraded expectations for 2012 though to 8% growth as economic activity turns higher following this year’s engineered slowdown. **Codelco records a 5.6% year-on-year increase in commercial copper output in Q1 2011** Codelco recorded a 5.6% year-on-year increase in its Q1 2011 commercial copper output, rising from 402.1kt to 424.8kt (including the company’s 49% stake in El Abra).
